questions.question: What mechanistic step accounts for the spontaneous conversion of open-chain D-glucose into glucopyranose in water?

options.label: A
options.text: Oxidation of the C6 alcohol to a carboxylic acid.

options.label: B
options.text: Homolytic cleavage of the C1-C2 single bond.

options.label: C
options.text: Intramolecular nucleophilic addition of the C5 hydroxyl oxygen to the electrophilic C1 aldehyde carbonyl to form a six-membered cyclic hemiacetal.

options.label: D
options.text: Intermolecular esterification between two glucose molecules.

questions.correct_answer: Intramolecular nucleophilic addition of the C5 hydroxyl oxygen to the electrophilic C1 aldehyde carbonyl to form a six-membered cyclic hemiacetal.
questions.explanation: The C5 hydroxyl attacks the C1 carbonyl in a 6-endo-trig cyclization, creating a new chiral anomeric center at C1.

questions.question: What is the chemical mechanism responsible for the mutarotation of pure α-D-glucopyranose in water until [α] = +52.7°?

options.label: A
options.text: Spontaneous epimerization at all five stereocenters simultaneously.

options.label: B
options.text: Dehydration of glucose into glucal.

options.label: C
options.text: Permanent decomposition of glucose into lactic acid.

options.label: D
options.text: Reversible acid/base-catalyzed ring opening through the acyclic aldehyde intermediate, followed by re-closure from either face to form an equilibrium mixture (36% α, 64% β).

questions.correct_answer: Reversible acid/base-catalyzed ring opening through the acyclic aldehyde intermediate, followed by re-closure from either face to form an equilibrium mixture (36% α, 64% β).
questions.explanation: Mutarotation occurs through reversible opening to the planar aldehyde, allowing re-closure from the top (β) or bottom (α) face.

questions.question: Why does treating D-glucose with anhydrous methanol and catalytic HCl lock the anomeric center (preventing mutarotation)?

options.label: A
options.text: The methyl group forms an ionic salt with chloride.

options.label: B
options.text: Acid protonates the anomeric C1-OH, which departs as water to form a resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion that is trapped by methanol as a stable acetal (methyl glucoside).

options.label: C
options.text: Methanol oxidizes the C1 carbon to an ester.

options.label: D
options.text: Methanol reacts with all six carbons simultaneously.

questions.correct_answer: Acid protonates the anomeric C1-OH, which departs as water to form a resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion that is trapped by methanol as a stable acetal (methyl glucoside).
questions.explanation: Converting the hemiacetal to a stable acetal locks the ring: acetals are stable to neutral water and cannot mutarotate without strong acid.

questions.question: Why does neutral bromine water (Br₂ / H₂O) selectively oxidize aldoses to aldonic acids without attacking ketoses?

options.label: A
options.text: Bromine selectively oxidizes the open-chain aldehyde group to a carboxylic acid via a hypobromite intermediate; ketoses lack a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon and react very slowly.

options.label: B
options.text: Bromine water is a chiral oxidizing agent.

options.label: C
options.text: Bromine water destroys all ketones by radical cleavage.

options.label: D
options.text: Aldoses precipitate from water with bromine.

questions.correct_answer: Bromine selectively oxidizes the open-chain aldehyde group to a carboxylic acid via a hypobromite intermediate; ketoses lack a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon and react very slowly.
questions.explanation: Br₂/H₂O is a mild, selective oxidant for the aldehyde group of aldoses, leaving primary alcohols and ketoses unoxidized under neutral conditions.

questions.topic: Nitric Acid Aldaric Acid Dicarboxylic Oxidation
questions.question: What structural transformation occurs when D-glucose is heated with concentrated nitric acid (HNO₃)?

options.label: A
options.text: Both the C1 aldehyde and the terminal C6 primary alcohol are oxidized to carboxylic acid groups, yielding dicarboxylic D-glucaric acid (an aldaric acid).

options.label: B
options.text: The glucose ring is cleaved into two glyceraldehyde molecules.

options.label: C
options.text: Glucose is completely combusted to carbon dioxide.

options.label: D
options.text: Only the secondary alcohols at C2-C4 are oxidized.

questions.correct_answer: Both the C1 aldehyde and the terminal C6 primary alcohol are oxidized to carboxylic acid groups, yielding dicarboxylic D-glucaric acid (an aldaric acid).
questions.explanation: Hot nitric acid is a vigorous oxidant that converts both terminal carbons (C1 aldehyde and C6 primary alcohol) into -COOH groups.

questions.topic: Tollens Test Enediol Tautomerism of Ketoses
questions.question: Why do ketoses (such as D-fructose) give a positive Tollens silver mirror test despite lacking an aldehyde group?

options.label: A
options.text: Under the basic conditions of Tollens reagent, fructose undergoes reversible enediol tautomerization (Lobry de Bruyn-van Ekenstein) to equilibrate with aldoses (glucose/mannose).

options.label: B
options.text: Basic Tollens reagent cleaves fructose into formaldehyde.

options.label: C
options.text: Silver ions oxidize ketone carbonyls directly.

options.label: D
options.text: Fructose contains a hidden aldehyde in its ester form.

questions.correct_answer: Under the basic conditions of Tollens reagent, fructose undergoes reversible enediol tautomerization (Lobry de Bruyn-van Ekenstein) to equilibrate with aldoses (glucose/mannose).
questions.explanation: Basic conditions promote keto-enol tautomerism via an enediol intermediate, isomerizing ketoses into oxidizable aldoses.

questions.question: What is the mechanistic outcome of adding HCN to D-arabinose in the Kiliani-Fischer synthesis?

options.label: A
options.text: Cyanide oxidizes arabinose to an aldaric acid.

options.label: B
options.text: Cyanide removes one carbon from the arabinose chain.

options.label: C
options.text: Only a single optically pure enantiomer is produced.

options.label: D
options.text: Cyanide attacks the C1 aldehyde carbonyl from both re- and si-faces, creating a new chiral center at C2 and producing an epimeric pair of diastereomeric cyanohydrins.

questions.correct_answer: Cyanide attacks the C1 aldehyde carbonyl from both re- and si-faces, creating a new chiral center at C2 and producing an epimeric pair of diastereomeric cyanohydrins.
questions.explanation: Nucleophilic addition of cyanide to the prochiral aldehyde generates two C2 diastereomers (epimers) that are subsequently hydrolyzed to elongated aldoses.

questions.question: What is the key chain-shortening elimination step in the Wohl degradation of an aldose?

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of carbon monoxide from an acyl radical.

options.label: B
options.text: Decarboxylation of a β-keto acid intermediate.

options.label: C
options.text: Homolytic cleavage of the C-C bond by peroxide.

options.label: D
options.text: Base-promoted elimination of cyanide (HCN) from the peracetylated aldoxime nitrile derivative, expelling C1 and releasing an aldose with one fewer carbon atom.

questions.correct_answer: Base-promoted elimination of cyanide (HCN) from the peracetylated aldoxime nitrile derivative, expelling C1 and releasing an aldose with one fewer carbon atom.
questions.explanation: The peracetylated cyanohydrin intermediate undergoes base-promoted retro-cyanohydrin elimination to release cyanide and the shortened aldose.

questions.question: In the exhaustive periodic acid (HIO₄) oxidation of methyl α-D-glucopyranoside, why is no formic acid produced from C1?

options.label: A
options.text: Acetals are cleaved to free aldehydes by periodic acid.

options.label: B
options.text: C1 is protected as a methyl acetal with no free adjacent hydroxyl; periodate cleaves between C2-C3 and C3-C4, consuming 2 moles of HIO₄ and releasing 1 mole of formic acid from C3.

options.label: C
options.text: Periodic acid cannot react with cyclic molecules.

options.label: D
options.text: C1 is oxidized to carbon dioxide gas.

questions.correct_answer: C1 is protected as a methyl acetal with no free adjacent hydroxyl; periodate cleaves between C2-C3 and C3-C4, consuming 2 moles of HIO₄ and releasing 1 mole of formic acid from C3.
questions.explanation: Protected anomeric acetals cannot undergo cleavage at C1, confining periodate oxidation to unprotected vicinal secondary diol positions.

questions.question: Why is sucrose a non-reducing sugar that fails to react with Tollens or Fehling's reagents?

options.label: A
options.text: Sucrose contains no oxygen atoms.

options.label: B
options.text: Sucrose is an antiaromatic molecule.

options.label: C
options.text: The glycosidic linkage connects the anomeric carbon of glucose (C1) directly to the anomeric carbon of fructose (C2), locking both hemiacetals as acetals with no free aldehyde/ketone.

options.label: D
options.text: Sucrose is insoluble in water.

questions.question: Why does neutral bromine water (Br₂ / H₂O) selectively oxidize aldoses to aldonic acids without attacking ketoses?

options.text: Bromine water destroys all ketones by radical cleavage.

options.text: Bromine selectively oxidizes the open-chain aldehyde group to a carboxylic acid via a hypobromite intermediate; ketoses lack a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon and react very slowly.

options.text: Aldoses precipitate from water with bromine.

questions.correct_answer: Bromine selectively oxidizes the open-chain aldehyde group to a carboxylic acid via a hypobromite intermediate; ketoses lack a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon and react very slowly.
questions.explanation: Br₂/H₂O is a mild, selective oxidant for the aldehyde group of aldoses, leaving primary alcohols and ketoses unoxidized under neutral conditions.
